title: How Much Do CEOs Matter?
text:
In 1972 the sociologists Stanley Lieberson and James O'Connor asked a blunt question: how much does a change of chief executive actually change a company's results? They gathered twenty years of data, from 1946 to 1965, on 167 large American corporations in 13 industries, recording their sales, net earnings and profit margins, as well as every change in their top leadership.

They then separated the possible causes of a company's results into layers: the year, which captured the state of the whole economy; the industry the company belonged to; the company's own lasting characteristics; and finally the arrival of a new leader.

The economy, the industry and the company itself explained most of the differences. Once those were accounted for, changes of leadership added relatively little to the explanation of sales and net earnings. Their effect was larger for profit margins, where leaders seemed to make more of a difference, especially when measured a few years after a new leader took over. The authors concluded that leaders work within powerful constraints set by their environment and organization.
lesson: Leaders matter, but less than they and others usually think. Respect the forces beyond your control, and focus on the decisions you can truly influence.
source: Lieberson, S., and O'Connor, J. F. (1972). Leadership and organizational performance: A study of large corporations. American Sociological Review, 37(2), 117-130.
caveat: Later researchers argued the method underestimated leaders' impact, and estimates of how much CEOs matter remain debated.
